title: Feinberg v. Pfeiffer Co.
summary: A board resolution promising a long-serving employee $200 a month for life whenever she chose to retire lacked consideration, because past service cannot be bargained for and she promised no further work, but her retirement from a well-paid job in reliance on it made the promise binding under Restatement § 90; the induced act was the 1949 retirement, not her later illness.
notes: Court: St. Louis Court of Appeals, Missouri (1959).

sections.Parties: Anna Sacks Feinberg, a former Pfeiffer employee who retired in reliance on the company’s promise of $200 a month for life, was the plaintiff and respondent. Pfeiffer Company, formerly S. Pfeiffer Manufacturing Company, a pharmaceutical maker whose board adopted the pension resolution and whose later management cut the payments, was the defendant and appellant. Commissioner Doerner wrote the opinion, which the St. Louis Court of Appeals adopted per curiam on March 17, 1959.
sections.Material Facts: Feinberg began working for Pfeiffer in 1910 at seventeen and by 1947 was bookkeeper, office manager and assistant treasurer. On December 27, 1947 the board, recognized her long, faithful service, raised her salary from $350 to $400 a month, and resolved that she could retire whenever she chose and receive $200 a month for life, while hoping she would keep working for many years. Her employment remained at will and she promised no future service, testifying she would have kept working without the resolution. She retired on June 30, 1949 at fifty-seven, healthy, after she and her husband calculated that his earnings plus the pension would support them. Pfeiffer paid $200 monthly until new management, advised that no obligation existed, sent a $100 check on April 1, 1956; she refused it and sued. At trial she was sixty-five and, after cancer surgery in November 1957, unable to work.
sections.Procedural History: Feinberg sued in the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis on the promise of $200 a month for life. The parties waived a jury, and the court entered judgment for $5,100 in accrued installments through trial plus interest. Pfeiffer appealed, challenging evidentiary rulings, the findings on reliance and the legal sufficiency of the promise. Missouri statutes required the appellate court to review the law and the evidence and enter the judgment the trial court should have entered; it affirmed, and rehearing and transfer to the Missouri Supreme Court were denied. The casebook prints the consideration discussion and the reliance discussion as two excerpts of this one opinion.
sections.Issue: Was the pension promise supported by consideration in Feinberg’s past service or her continued employment? If not, did her retirement in reliance on the promise make it binding under promissory estoppel, notwithstanding the company’s argument that her later disability, not the promise, explained her inability to work?
sections.Holding: Past service was not consideration, because acts already performed cannot be sought in exchange for a later promise, and continued employment was not, because the resolution let her retire immediately and she promised no further work. Retirement, however, was action the company should reasonably have expected its resolution to induce, and the promise did induce it: she gave up a lucrative position while still able to work. Under § 90 of the First Restatement the promise was binding because injustice could be avoided only by enforcement. The $5,100 judgment plus interest was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Pfeiffer adopted the pension after thirty-seven years of service; those completed acts had been rendered under the existing employment and could not have been the price of a promise made in 1947. Nor did the following eighteen months of work: the resolution allowed immediate retirement and attached no service condition. Retirement was different. Section 90 of the First Restatement binds a promise the promisor should reasonably expect to induce definite and substantial action or forbearance that it does induce, when only enforcement can avoid injustice. The board deliberately created a retirement privilege exercisable whenever Feinberg chose, so retirement was the very conduct the promise invited; the trial judge credited her testimony that she could have kept working and planned her household around the pension. Injustice followed from the surrender of a well-paid position at fifty-seven and nearly seven years of payments before the company tried to halve them, by which time comparable employment was realistically unavailable. Her 1957 cancer strengthened the consequences but did not control enforceability, since the induced act was the 1949 retirement. The court treated Ricketts v. Scothorn as closely analogous.

Court: St. Louis Court of Appeals, Missouri (1959).

The same entry combines both assigned excerpts without treating the consideration rejection as the case’s ultimate outcome. Past services and past consideration, reliance on a later promise, and a later medical condition play different roles.

sections.Parties: Feinberg, a longtime employee, sued Pfeiffer Company for pension payments promised in a board resolution.
sections.Material Facts: After many years of service, Feinberg received a salary increase and the right to retire at any time with $200 per month for life. She was not required to work for a further fixed period. She retired about eighteen months later, at age fifty-seven, in reliance on the pension. The company paid until it later attempted to reduce the amount. By that time she was older and less able to obtain new work.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for $5,100 in unpaid installments. The Missouri appellate decision is divided between an initial consideration excerpt and a later reliance excerpt. The court affirmed the judgment on the reliance ground.
sections.Issue: Were past services or voluntary continued work consideration for the pension, and could retirement induced by the assurance supply a different basis of enforcement?
sections.Holding: Past services were not bargained for in exchange for the later promise, and future service was not required by its terms. Retirement in reliance on the pension made the promise enforceable under the court’s promissory-estoppel analysis.
sections.Reasoning: The resolution’s operation permitted immediate retirement, so subsequent service cannot be inserted as a condition that the board never demanded. The later excerpt focuses on the employee’s induced choice to leave work and the difficulty of reversing that choice after years had passed. Subsequent illness was not the act of reliance: the promise induced retirement. The notes’ Hayes comparison asks what changes if the employee had already decided to retire before receiving the pension assurance.

topics.promissory-estoppel: The pension induced retirement and a lasting change of position.
topics.consideration: Past service and hoped-for future service were not bargained for.
topics.reliance: The relevant induced act was retirement, not later illness.
topics.reliance-damages: The court enforced the promised installments; reliance does not invariably mean recovery limited to expenses.
